_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: He said to him: he is not liable.
rashi:a1.2: Do we read of it, “If the place be too far from you, then you shall slaughter”: for it is from there that we derive that it is forbidden to slaughter non-sacred animals in the Temple courtyard. We expound: when the place is far you slaughter [for ordinary meat], but you do not slaughter when the place is near, in the courtyard; in the second chapter of Kiddushin (57b). And here, do we read it so? He cannot slaughter this animal anywhere but in the courtyard, since it is a peace offering.
rashi:a2.1: It is non-sacred and its offspring is a peace offering: according to the one who says that sanctity takes effect on fetuses. And he slaughtered the mother outside: is he liable to karet for the fetus, on account of slaughtering [offerings] outside?
rashi:a3.1: Do we read of it, “That they may bring them to the Lord”: for one is liable for slaughtering outside only for those that are fit for an offering, and this fetus is not fit for an offering now.
rashi:a3.2: “That they may bring them to the Lord”: this is written about slaughtering outside.
rashi:a5.1: MISHNA. A mixture renders a mixture only according to calculation: this is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a6.1: And leavened dough leavens only according to calculation: non-sacred dough that was leavened with teruma leaven is entirely forbidden. If some of that dough fell into another non-sacred dough and leavened it, it forbids it only according to the calculation of the teruma leaven mixed into it. That is, if so much of the first dough fell into the last that it contains enough of the teruma leaven [the first] was leavened with to leaven the last, the last is forbidden too. But if what fell from the first into the last, all of it together, has only enough to leaven the last, the last is permitted, since not enough of the teruma fell into it to leaven it.
rashi:a6.2: Drawn water: this is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a7.1: And the water of purification becomes water of purification only with the placing of the ashes: at the moment one places the ashes, it becomes water of purification. Therefore the water must be in the vessel first and the ashes afterward. But if he placed the ashes first and then the water, it is unfit, since at the placing of the ashes, which makes the water of purification, there was no water there, and it can no longer become water of purification.
rashi:a7.2: And a beit haperas does not make a beit haperas: a field in which a grave was plowed; [the name comes] from “something spread out [paros].” If he went on and plowed the beit haperas and the fields around it, we do not presume the other fields to be a beit haperas on the chance that the plow carried bones into the fields around it, since one grave makes a beit haperas only to the measure explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a7.3: And there is no teruma after teruma: if he separated teruma and then separated again, the second is not teruma.
rashi:a9.1: GEMARA. Who is the tanna: of “a mixture renders a mixture only according to calculation”?
rashi:a10.1: It renders it a mixture as definite teruma does: so that if a se’a of the mixture fell elsewhere, and there are not one hundred se’a there besides this se’a, all of it is forbidden.
rashi:a10.2: Since I say that the se’a that fell: into the mixture is the very se’a that came up and fell again into the other [produce].
rashi:a11.1: Only according to the calculation within it: according to how much teruma is in this se’a of the mixture, we require one hundred such measures of non-sacred produce; we do not require one hundred se’a. For example: a se’a of teruma first fell into twenty-four se’a of non-sacred produce and they became a mixture; now every se’a there is one twenty-fourth teruma, that is, a log of teruma in each se’a. If a se’a of that mixture then fell into other non-sacred produce, and there are seventy-seven other log of non-sacred produce there, they combine with the twenty-four log of non-sacred produce in this se’a and nullify the log of teruma.
rashi:a12.1: And leavened dough does not leaven, etc., not in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer: for Rabbi Eliezer does not require that there be enough of the forbidden [leaven] to leaven; rather the forbidden and the permitted combine to forbid it.
rashi:a13.1: I follow the last: since it is what causes the leavening, and if the forbidden fell last, the dough is forbidden. And [as for] our mishna: even though only enough to leaven fell from the first dough into the last, so that most of the leavening was non-sacred, Rabbi Eliezer still forbids it, since he holds that where this and that together cause [the result], it is forbidden. And “I follow the last,” which Rabbi Eliezer says, is not meant precisely: even if the forbidden fell first and the permitted afterward, if he did not first remove the forbidden but left it, and the two together leavened the dough, it is forbidden. For Rabbi Eliezer holds “this and that cause it: forbidden,” in the first chapter of Bekhorot (7a) and likewise everywhere. And so Abaye answered in Pesaḥim, chapter Kol Sha’a (27a): they taught this only where he first removed the forbidden, but if he did not, it is forbidden. And although a difficulty is raised there about this, in the end the conclusion of that discussion is that Rabbi Eliezer holds “this and that cause it: forbidden.”
rashi:a14.1: Rainwater: is fit for immersion, for we require living [spring] water only for a zav.
rashi:a14.2: One fills by the shoulder: nineteen se’a of drawn water.
rashi:a14.3: And lets it flow into the ritual bath: he must not pour from the bucket into the ritual bath, for in that way it would be invalidated even by three log. Rather he makes a channel and a hollow some distance away, pours from the bucket into the hollow, and the water runs through the channel into the ritual bath. This is “drawing [hamshakha].”
tosafot:a5.1: A mixture renders a mixture again only according to calculation: as the Gemara explains, for example a se’a of teruma fell into less than one hundred of non-sacred produce and they became a mixture, and some of the mixture fell elsewhere. It renders the second a mixture only according to the calculation of the teruma in it: if the second contains enough to nullify the measure of teruma that fell into it, it is nullified, even though the first did not contain enough to nullify the teruma that fell into it. This is like the Rabbis in the Gemara and not like Rabbi Eliezer, who said it renders a mixture as teruma does. And Rabbi Eliezer’s ruling applies even if the second contains one hundred, enough to nullify what fell into it, since [a se’a] was not lifted out of [the first] before it fell into the second, and it must be lifted out because of robbery of the tribe [of priests].
tosafot:a6.1: And leavened dough leavens again only according to calculation: Rashi explained: non-sacred dough leavened with teruma leaven is entirely forbidden; if some of that dough fell into another non-sacred dough and leavened it, it forbids it only according to the calculation of the teruma leaven mixed into it; that is, if so much of the first fell into the last that it contains enough of the teruma leaven to leaven the last, the last is forbidden too, and if all that fell from the first into the last has only enough to leaven the last, the last is permitted, since not enough of the teruma fell into it to leaven it. End of Rashi’s words. But this does not seem right. For if so, when the Gemara says of it, “Not in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer, as we learned: Non-sacred leaven and teruma leaven, etc.,” why must it bring [the mishna about leaven] to show it is not like Rabbi Eliezer? It could have proved that well from the mishna it brought for the mixture. Therefore it seems right to explain: for example, an olive-bulk of teruma leaven and an olive-bulk of non-sacred leaven, both intact, fell into a non-sacred dough and leavened it, and neither alone had enough to leaven it: the dough is not forbidden. That is “according to calculation”: enough to leaven from the teruma leaven alone. This is exactly the mishna the Gemara brings for it, “And the Rabbis say, etc.,” [against Rabbi Eliezer,] who holds that where this and that cause it, it is forbidden.
tosafot:a14.1: And drawn water invalidates the ritual bath only according to calculation, [etc.]: it is Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov, as we learned, etc.: for drawn water is purified by a majority and by flowing. And that is “according to calculation”: drawn water invalidates only if it equals the fit water, that is, twenty se’a of drawn and twenty se’a of fit. But if he let only nineteen se’a of drawn water flow into twenty-one of fit, it is fit.
gershom:a1.1: And its offspring is a peace offering: is one liable for its fetus on account of slaughtering outside? Do we read of the fetus, “That they may bring them to the Lord”? It cannot be brought, so he is exempt.
gershom:a2.1: Another version: “fit for the entrance of the Tent” to be brought: for that, one is liable outside. And this [mother], since it is non-sacred, is not fit for the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, for just as “Mine in yours” is forbidden [consecrated animals slaughtered outside], so “yours in Mine” is forbidden: it is forbidden to slaughter non-sacred animals inside. Therefore he is exempt.
gershom:a3.1: And he slaughtered it inside, what is the law? Is he liable on account of the fetus? [This is Abaye’s question from 11b, which Rav Yosef answers here.]
gershom:a4.1: (This belongs to the previous amud.) He said to him: Do we read of it [the printed text adds, in parentheses, “That they may bring them to the Lord”] “If the place be too far from you, then you shall slaughter”? That is: what you slaughter when the place is far, outside, you eat as non-sacred; and you do not eat what you slaughter when the place is near, that is, non-sacred animals slaughtered inside. For this [fetus] is not something one slaughters.
gershom:a5.1: A mixture renders a mixture only according to the calculation of the teruma in it, as the Gemara explains: a se’a of teruma fell into less than one hundred, for example into twenty se’a of non-sacred produce. For the law of teruma is that if it fell into one hundred of non-sacred produce it is nullified, and here it fell into less than one hundred, such as twenty se’a of non-sacred produce. And [some] of that mixture went and fell elsewhere, for example a se’a of that mixture fell again into eighty se’a of non-sacred produce.
gershom:a6.1: Rabbi Eliezer says: It renders a mixture as definite teruma does. That is, that se’a of the mixture [made when the teruma] fell into twenty of non-sacred: we regard that se’a of the mixture as if it were a se’a of definite teruma, not dissolved among those twenty of non-sacred. For I say: the se’a of teruma that fell into those less than one hundred is the very se’a that came up and fell again elsewhere, into those eighty of non-sacred, and it is not nullified in eighty of non-sacred.
gershom:a7.1: And the Rabbis say: it renders a mixture only according to calculation. That is, we do not regard the se’a that fell as the very one that came up; rather that se’a holds only one twentieth teruma and the rest non-sacred. Now that it fell into eighty of non-sacred, it is mixed into one hundred of non-sacred and is nullified. And that is “only according to calculation” that our mishna says, not in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer.
gershom:a8.1: Dough leavened with [leaven] leavens only according to calculation: as it is explained, non-sacred leaven and teruma leaven, that is, the forbidden kind.
gershom:a9.1: Rabbi Eliezer says: I follow the last. That is, if the permitted fell last, it nullified the first, forbidden one, and it is as if all were permitted; and if the forbidden fell last, it nullified the first, permitted one, and we regard it as if all were forbidden. And the Rabbis say: whether the forbidden fell first or last, it is not forbidden unless the forbidden [leaven] has enough to leaven by itself, without the non-sacred one. And this is “only according to calculation” that the mishna says, not in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer.
gershom:a10.1: Drawn water invalidates the ritual bath only according to calculation: as explained, unless most of it is drawn water. As we learned: a ritual bath that has twenty-one se’a [of rainwater, for rainwater is fit for immersion for all who must immerse except zavim; one fills by the shoulder nineteen se’a of drawn water] and lets it flow into the ritual bath: he pours it outside, [beside] the ritual bath, and makes [for it] a channel [like a gutter]; “lets it flow” means he draws it into the ritual bath through that gutter.
rashi:b1.1: And they are pure: that is, the bath is fit to immerse in.
rashi:b1.2: Drawn water is purified by a majority and by flowing: when the majority is rainwater that fell into it by itself, and he let a minority of drawn water flow into it through a channel, the drawn water is purified. And this is the mishna’s “according to calculation”: drawn water that flows in does not invalidate the ritual bath unless there were twenty se’a of it.
rashi:b2.1: By inference, the Rabbis, etc.: that is, since you say our mishna is Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov and not the Rabbis, and the mishna is lenient, as it is phrased in the language of leniency, “drawn water invalidates only according to calculation,” by inference the Rabbis disagree in the direction of stringency.
rashi:b2.2: But that which Ravin said when he came: drawn water that one let flow, all of it, is fit: even an entire ritual bath of drawn water, if it flowed in, is fit. [That accords with] neither Rabbi Eliezer [ben Ya’akov] nor the Rabbis.
rashi:b3.1: Rather, Rav Pappa said [Rashi’s text reads Rav Pappa; the printed Gemara has Rabba]: the Rabbis disagree in the direction of leniency, and Ravin’s report when he came is the Rabbis’ view. And our mishna is not dealing with this, that you should say it is Rabbi Eliezer [ben Ya’akov] and the Rabbis disagree in the direction of stringency.
rashi:b3.2: Only according to the calculation of the vessels, and it is Yosef ben Ḥoni.
rashi:b4.1: That fell into the ritual bath: from the vessel into the ritual bath, by flowing.
rashi:b4.2: From two or three vessels: where a whole log fell from each vessel, it invalidates. But from four or five vessels, where no whole log falls at once, they did not invalidate it. And the mishna’s “according to calculation” means this too.
rashi:b5.1: (Only with the placing of the ashes: at the time the ashes are placed it becomes water of purification. Evidently the water must come first, for if the water came last it would not be water of purification, since at the time the ashes were placed it did not become water of purification, as there was no water there.)
rashi:b5.2: Not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon: for according to Rabbi Shimon, if he put the ashes before the water, it is fit.
rashi:b6.1: As it is taught: about the sota, if he put the dust from the floor into the vessel before the water, it is unfit, etc.
rashi:b7.1: And we said: What is the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon? As it is written: about the water of purification, “And for the impure they shall take of the dust,” and it is taught, etc.
rashi:b8.1: It is stated here: with the water of purification, “dust,” and it is stated with the sota, “dust.” Just as with the sota the dust goes on the water, as it is written (Numbers 5:17), “And of the dust that is on [the floor of the Tabernacle], etc.,” so here, dust on top of the water. And this is the proper performance of its mitzva from the outset.
rashi:b8.2: And just as here, etc.: as the Gemara goes on to explain, “And here, from where do we derive it?” Evidently Rabbi Shimon holds that with the water of purification, if he put the dust before the water, it is fit.
rashi:b9.1: And it is written, “Running water in a vessel”: which implies that the water is to be put into a vessel and not onto the dust, for “in a vessel” implies that dust first is unfit.
rashi:b10.1: He is required to mix them: “and place on it” does not come to say that if he put the dust first it is fit, but to say that one must take care, after putting the dust onto the water, to mix them well with his finger and bring the water beneath it back up over it.
rashi:b11.1: And say that the first clause of the verse is specific: that the ashes come before the water, as it is written, “and place on it [running] water.” And “in a vessel” comes to teach that its “running” [freshness] be in the vessel: that he not fill the water in another vessel and pour it into this one, but put this vessel into the spring and take the water into it.
rashi:b11.2: And it answers: just as we find in every place: for example with the sota, the dust is above, for it alone is what makes the water fit, and it is above. For everyone agrees that the mitzva [with the sota] is to put the water first, as it is written, “And of the dust, etc.”
rashi:b11.3: So here, the facilitating item above: therefore, of necessity, the last clause of the verse is meant for itself, and the first clause is for the exposition, to mix them.
rashi:b12.1: Rabbi Eliezer says: A beit haperas makes a beit haperas: all four fields around the beit haperas are [a beit haperas] if they were plowed, since the soil of the beit haperas renders them impure.
tosafot:b3.1: In brief: “Rather, Rav Pappa said: according to the calculation of the vessels”: that is, the three log fell from three vessels, matching the count of log, and it is Yosef ben Ḥoni. On this reading the Rabbis disagree in the direction of leniency, Ravin’s report is the Rabbis’ view, and our mishna does not deal with that case, that one should say it is Rabbi Eliezer [ben Ya’akov] and the Rabbis are stringent. So Rashi explains. Rabbi Shmuel of Lunel objected: (1) This is not the Talmud’s way: at first, according to Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba, Rabbi Eliezer [ben Ya’akov] is lenient and the Rabbis stringent, and according to Ravina [so Tosafot here] Rabbi Eliezer is stringent and the Rabbis lenient; we do not find Amoraim reversing a view like this. (2) How could the Rabbis hold that a bath made entirely of drawn water that flowed in, with no other rainwater, is fit? That would be difficult from Ta’anit (13a), which seeks support for permitting cold bathing [on fast days] from “all who must immerse do so as usual on Tisha B’Av and Yom Kippur,” arguing that there is no immersion in hot water, since hot water is drawn; on Rashi’s reading, hot water could be made fit by flowing. (3) From Mikvaot (6:8): two baths, an upper one of forty se’a and a lower one lacking forty; one fills by the shoulder and pours into the upper one until forty se’a run down to the lower. If flowing alone purified drawn water, why pour into the upper bath? He could pour it on the ground and let it flow. (4) From Mikvaot (4:4): rainwater and drawn water that mixed in a courtyard, a pit or on the steps of the cave: if most is fit, it is fit; if most is unfit, it is unfit; half and half, unfit; when? when they mixed before reaching the bath. Why would mixing matter, if drawn water alone is made fit by flowing? Rabbi Shmuel sent that he had received from his teachers that “drawn water that one let flow, all of it, is pure” means when forty se’a of rainwater then come into the bath. That answers everything, and Ravin’s statement then fits Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov, who requires a fit majority for making up forty se’a. The She’iltot of Rav Aḥai implies the same: three log of drawn water that fell into a bath invalidate it, but if one let them run outside through a gutter into the bath they do not, as Ravin reported, and they combine toward forty se’a, as Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov taught; so the two statements do not conflict. The Ri replied that our passage can be explained well [as Rashi does]: the Gemara understood that Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov requires a majority of rainwater, and if most is drawn, even forty se’a of rainwater coming afterward do not make it fit; that is why it objects that Ravin’s statement fits neither. And the Ri says none of the objections is difficult. (1) In several places the Talmud first explains a tanna as stringent and then as lenient, as in Kiddushin (37a) on “Rabbi Eliezer says: also new grain,” where it asks whether he disagrees leniently or stringently. (2) Ta’anit is no difficulty, for it would be difficult on your view too: hot water is possible by letting nineteen se’a of hot water flow into twenty-one of rainwater, or with heated iron bars placed in the bath, as in Yoma (31b) about the High Priest’s immersion on Yom Kippur. (3) The other Mikvaot mishnayot can be set according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov; and the case of the upper and lower baths teaches that where a bath already holds forty se’a of fit water, even one hundred se’a of drawn water do not invalidate it. The practical conclusion that seems right: one should not make a bath entirely of drawn water by flowing, for even on Rashi’s reading the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov, whose teaching is “a small measure, but clean.” But by majority and flowing it is fit according to all: if a bath holds twenty-one se’a of fit water, one may fill nineteen se’a by the shoulder, pour them into a channel in the ground and let them flow into the bath until it is full, as in Mikvaot chapter 4 (“when? when they mixed before reaching the bath”), since we concluded that by majority and flowing it is fit according to all. And “mixed before reaching the bath” comes to exclude a pipe that was carved and only afterward fixed in place, which runs down into the bath without flowing [through the ground]. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b4.1: Yosef ben Ḥoni says: in two or three vessels they invalidate the ritual bath; in four or five vessels they do not: and the mishna’s “according to calculation” means this: drawn water invalidates the ritual bath only if it fell from vessels matching the count of log that invalidate the bath, that is, three; but if the three log fell in four or five times, they do not invalidate it. And Rabbi Avraham ben David [the Ra’avad] ruled that the halakha follows Yosef ben Ḥoni. It therefore seems that when people bail out a ritual bath to clean it, taking out the water in it, and other water comes in its place, there is no concern even if a little of the bailed water remains in the bath. Although it falls back from the bucket into the bath, and there are more than three log of drawn water there, still there is no concern, for presumably the three log did not fall from three vessels. And some are stringent and pierce the bucket with a hole that lets liquid in, because of the concern I explained.
tosafot:b9.1: How so? If he wishes, dust below; if he wishes, dust above: And if you ask: if so, what does the verbal analogy come for? One can say: for the mitzva [from the outset] we require water first and then dust, as it is written with the sota (Numbers 5:17), “And of the dust that is on the floor of the Tabernacle the priest shall take and put it into the water”; and for that the verbal analogy comes.
gershom:b1.1: And they are pure: and they lose the status of drawn water, for drawn water is purified by the majority, if most of the bath is not drawn, and by flowing, that is, “and lets it flow,” as we said.
gershom:b2.1: By inference, the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov hold that it is not nullified by a majority and flowing.
gershom:b3.1: But that which, when (Rav Dimi) [Ravin] came, he said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: [drawn water that one let flow, all of it, that is, all forty se’a in this manner, is pure: whose view is it? Neither the Rabbis nor Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov.] Rather, Rav Pappa said [so Rabbeinu Gershom; the printed Gemara has Rabba]: what is “only according to calculation” that it says? It means according to the calculation of the vessels, and like Yosef ben Ḥoni.
gershom:b4.1: As it is taught: three log of drawn water that fell into the ritual bath directly, without flowing, whether those three log were in two vessels or three, or in four or five, and fell into the ritual bath: they invalidate it.
gershom:b5.1: Yosef ben Ḥoni says: if those three log were in two or three vessels and fell into it, they invalidate it, since each vessel holds a log or more, which is significant and invalidates. But if those three log were divided among four or five vessels, so that no vessel holds a log or more, it is not significant enough to invalidate the ritual bath. Another version, as written in the last clause: “But that which, when Rav Dimi came, he said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: drawn water, etc.”
gershom:b6.1: Whose view? [It cannot be said to be] the Rabbis, the first tanna who disputes Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov, [as lenient,] for if it were the Rabbis, why would Rabbi Eliezer [ben Ya’akov] say “only according to calculation”? [By inference the Rabbis are stringent:] “only according to calculation” implies that with less than this [the Rabbis] invalidate the ritual bath. Rather, conclude from Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov’s saying “only according to calculation” [that the Rabbis disagree in the direction of stringency]. And if so, Ravin’s report when he came, etc., accords with neither. Rather, “only according to calculation” is not Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov but the calculation of vessels, and it is Yosef ben Ḥoni, etc. And this is like the first version. [The printed text here carries several editorial corrections; this follows the corrected reading.]
gershom:b7.1: Only with the placing of the ashes: that is, only when he puts the ashes on top of the water. But is it not ashes, the ash of the heifer? [And “dust” is stated there: “And of the dust that is on the floor of the Tabernacle.”] And it is written, “running water in a vessel,” that is, the water [goes] into the vessel specifically. And when the verse says, “and place on it water,” that is, on the dust, [it is not written for this]; rather it is written to mix the dust and the water [together], and in fact the water comes first. And from where [do we know] that it is so, as the Rabbis say, [and not perhaps as Rabbi Shimon says]? Because just as we find in every place, [with the sota the facilitating item is above, as it is written, “And of the dust that is on the floor of the Tabernacle the priest shall take and put it into the water,” the facilitating item above, so here too].
gershom:b8.1: Another version: and the first tanna, [who disputes] Rabbi Shimon, holds that the last clause of the verse, “running water in a vessel,” is specific. And this is like the first version.
